document.title: Comments of Edison Electric Institute re PJM Governance and Stakeholder Reform
document.group: PJM governance and stakeholder reform vote

pages.text:
1 
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
PJM Governance and Stakeholder Reforms 
 
Docket No.  AD26-7-000 
COMMENTS OF THE EDISON ELECTRIC INSTITUTE 
Edison Electric Institute (“EEI”) respectfully submits these comments regarding 
governance and stakeholder reforms in PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”).1   
EEI’s member companies are the nation’s investor-owned electric utilities.  
Together, we provide electricity to nearly 250 million Americans, operate in all 50 states 
and the District of Columbia, and support over seven million jobs in communities across 
the country.  EEI member companies work every day to provide reliable energy to their 
customers at the lowest cost possible.  EEI member companies also form the backbone of 
our nation’s electric power industry, which is essential to advancing our economic and 
national security priorities.  Over the next five years, investor-owned electric companies 
will invest more than $1.3 trillion to enhance the electric grid, building critically needed 
new generation and transmission and distribution infrastructure required to power 
economic prosperity. 
EEI commends the Commission for undertaking a structured effort to reform PJM’s 
governance and stakeholder processes.  This initiative is timely and necessary, arriving at 
a genuine inflection point in PJM’s history.  The issues being confronted in this proceeding 
 
1 See PJM Governance & Stakeholder Reforms, Notice Requesting Post-Conf. Comment, Docket 
No. AD26-7-000 (July 30, 2026).

2 
have persisted for more than a decade yet went largely unaddressed, as PJM’s wholesale 
market conditions yielded surplus capacity in an era of flat or declining load.  Those 
conditions masked PJM’s governance and structural resource adequacy flaws. 
Today, the region is experiencing capacity scarcity in the face of significant growth.  
PJM’s unwieldy governance structures cannot produce the types of bold market reforms 
required to transform today’s challenges into opportunity for the region.  There is an acute 
need for “concrete, actionable reforms to improve PJM’s ability to address operational and 
market needs in a timely and efficient manner.”2   
We file these comments to underscore one message:  governance reforms in PJM 
are a necessary and important, but insufficient, step.  An improved, more transparent 
stakeholder process cannot procure the new capacity that is needed to meet customer needs 
in PJM.  For this reason, governance reforms must proceed alongside—and in service of—
market reforms.  EEI members stand ready to tackle these interrelated challenges.   
I. 
PJM’S GOVERNANCE STRUCTURES FAIL TO DELIVER TIMELY, 
IMPACTFUL SOLUTIONS TO THE CRISIS FACING PJM’S MARKETS 
Conditions within PJM have fundamentally changed in recent years due to several 
factors, creating urgency for meaningful reform.  After years of stagnation, demand growth 
is accelerating again.  Summer peak load growth is now projected to average 2.4 percent 
per year over twenty years, while winter peak load growth is projected to average 2.7 
 
2 PJM Governance and Stakeholder Reforms, Second Suppl. Notice of Commission-Led Tech. 
Conf., Docket No. AD26-7-000, at 1 (July 2, 2026).

3 
percent per year over the same period.3  The causes of this growth are well known:  rapidly 
increasing demand for artificial intelligence infrastructure, including data centers, in 
addition to advanced manufacturing and broader electrification.4  Serving this new demand 
while protecting other electricity customers is critical for national security and economic 
development across the region.5  But demand is outpacing the market’s ability to bring on 
new supply options—a troubling dynamic exacerbated by supply chain constraints.  The 
result is a resource adequacy shortfall that PJM leadership anticipates will “persist for some 
time.”6 
The pressure that demand growth has placed on PJM’s resource adequacy construct, 
and the risks that it creates, are not theoretical.  Since January 2025, PJM has entered into 
NERC EEA emergency alert conditions multiple times,7 and has sought and received 
 
3 PJM INTERCONNECTION, LLC, 2026 PJM Load Forecast Rep., at 6 (Jan. 14, 2026), 
https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/library/reports-notices/load-forecast/2026-load-
report.pdf. 
4 See PJM Governance & Stakeholder Reforms, Pre-Filed Statement of Stacey Burbure on Behalf 
of Am. Elec. Power Co., Inc., Docket No. AD26-7-000, at 3 (filed July 15, 2026) (“July 15, 2026 
Pre-Filed Statement of Stacey Burbure”). 
5 Id.  
6 PJM INTERCONNECTION, LLC, Powering Reliability Through Mkt. Design, at 4 (May 6, 2026) 
(“Powering Reliability”), https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/library/reports-notices/special-
reports/2026/20260506-powering-reliability-through-market-design.pdf. 
7 Per PJM’s Emergency Procedures website, PJM issued RTO-wide NERC EEA alerts on January 
21, 2025; between June 22-24, 2025; between July 14-15, 2025; between July 23-24, 2025; 
between July 27-29, 2025; on January 26, 2026; between May 17-19, 2026; between June 30, 2026 
and July 2, 2026; and between July 14-15, 2026.

4 
multiple emergency authorizations from the U.S. Department of Energy to preserve 
reliability.8   
EEI applauds the operational excellence of PJM personnel who have navigated these 
difficult conditions.  But frequent emergency conditions underscore how little margin 
remains in the system. 
Addressing this challenge will require near-term measures, as well as longer-term, 
fundamental changes to PJM’s stakeholder and governance processes.  As PJM recognizes, 
the stakeholder process was not “built for speed or operational agility”—the very 
capabilities that current conditions demand.9  The process is slow, opaque, and vulnerable 
to quagmire.10  The result is oftentimes deadlock, producing incremental adjustments when 
decisive action is needed.  EEI does not offer this observation as criticism, but as 
 
8 See U.S. Dep’t of Energy, Order Authorizing Emergency Grid Reliability Actions, Docket No. 
202-26-02 (Jan. 25, 2026) (authorizing PJM to direct generating units to operate up to maximum 
output notwithstanding environmental emissions limitations during Winter Storm Fern); U.S. 
Dep’t of Energy, Order Authorizing Deployment of Backup Generation Res., Docket No. 202-26-
06 (Jan. 26, 2026) (permitting PJM to dispatch data center backup generation); U.S. Dep’t of 
Energy, Order Authorizing Emergency Grid Reliability Actions, Docket No. 202-26-23 (May 18, 
2026) (permitting PJM to dispatch data center backup generation); U.S. Dep’t of Energy, Order 
Authorizing Emergency Operations, Docket No. 202-26-35 (July 14, 2026) (granting PJM 
authority to dispatch permit-limited units and backup generation). 
9 See PJM Governance & Stakeholder Reforms, Comments from PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 
Docket No. AD26-7-000, at 1 (filed July 14, 2026). 
10 See FERC, Chairman Laura Swett’s Comments at PJM’s Annual Meeting in Baltimore, MD, at 
2 (May 12, 2026) (observing that the “current stakeholder process is slow where it must be fast, 
opaque where it must be transparent, and vulnerable to vetoes and agenda control exactly when 
the region needs immediate action”); see also PJM Governance & Stakeholder Reforms, Pre-filed 
Statement of Jodi L. Moskowitz on Behalf of the PSEG Companies, Docket No. AD26-7-000, at 
2 (filed July 14, 2026) (“July 14 Pre-filed Statement of Jodi L. Moskowitz”) (citation omitted).

5 
recognition of our shared challenge.  For these reasons, EEI fully supports the Commission 
moving forward in a structured and time-bound manner in cooperation with states. 
II. 
GOVERNANCE AND STAKEHOLDER REFORMS ARE NECESSARY BUT 
INSUFFICIENT TO MEET THE RESOURCE ADEQUACY CHALLENGE 
While governance and stakeholder reform is essential, resolving these challenges 
will not, by itself, solve the larger and more critical resource adequacy problems facing the 
region.  The core problem confronting PJM in 2026 is underinvestment in generation.  And 
there is a real risk that conditions could deteriorate before they improve.  Accordingly, 
governance reform is a necessary first step.  But governance reform must be in service of 
facilitating genuine reforms to address the underlying supply shortfall. 
A. 
The resource adequacy challenge threatens PJM’s fundamental charge 
to serve customers reliably 
PJM’s “core responsibility” is maintaining reliability.11  And PJM has long 
“operated on the principle that all customers share in a common standard of reliability and 
willingness to pay to meet it.”12  But current resource adequacy conditions are undermining 
PJM’s ability to meet these standards.  The problem is documented in PJM’s own 
“Powering Reliability Through Market Design” whitepaper and in comments filed in this 
docket.13  PJM explains that the current shortage is structural rather than cyclical—not a 
temporary supply gap that will close on its own, but the predictable result of several 
 
11 PJM INTERCONNECTION, LLC, Interim Res. Adequacy Serv. Proposal (Aug. 13, 2026), 
https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/about-pjm/newsroom/fact-sheets/interim-resource-
adequacy-service-proposal.pdf. 
12 Powering Reliability at 6.  
13 See generally id.; see also July 14, 2026 Pre-filed Statement of Jodi L. Moskowitz at 3-4; July 
15, 2026 Pre-Filed Statement of Stacey Burbure at 2.

6 
structural shifts occurring at once.14  Demand is surging faster than supply has followed.  
The timing gap between when demand arrives and when supply responds lies at the very 
core of the shortage.  Compounding the problem, PJM observes that building new 
generation now costs roughly twice as much and takes twice as long as before.15  Capital 
costs for a new combined-cycle plant have roughly doubled and those for a combustion 
turbine have increased by more than fifty percent, even as supply chain backlogs, 
permitting timelines, and equipment scarcity show every sign of persisting.16  In short, the 
barriers to entry are far higher today than when the market was designed. 
The consequences of the resource adequacy gap are visible in the region’s core 
reliability metrics.  For example, the 2027/28 Base Residual Auction failed to procure 
sufficient capacity to satisfy the required reserve margin, clearing at an Installed Reserve 
Margin of 14.4 percent—5.6 percentage points below PJM’s 20 percent reliability target—
and leaving a physical deficit of more than 6,000 MW.17  That shortfall places direct 
pressure on the region's long-standing “1-in-10” loss-of-load standard, which, absent 
corrective action, risks eroding into a far weaker level of service for every customer.18 
 
14 Powering Reliability at 9-10 (describing “a rapid convergence of three structural forces”—
surging demand, accelerated retirements, and supply-chain and permitting frictions—and the 
resulting “transition from an era of managing surplus to an era of managing scarcity”); see also id. 
at 16 (“PJM is facing a period of structural scarcity, a fundamental mismatch between how fast 
demand is growing and how fast new supply can follow.”). 
15 Id. at 16. 
16 Id. at 16-20. 
17 Id. at 16. 
18 Powering Reliability at 37-38 (explaining how, absent corrective action, service will continue to 
degrade).

7 
B. 
New supply in PJM has been slow to come online despite record-high 
capacity auction prices 
The existing PJM resource adequacy construct cannot address the current resource 
adequacy shortfall.  New supply has been slow to come online despite record-high capacity 
auction prices.  Recent Base Residual Auction results demonstrate the shortfall in new 
capacity.  The 2027/28 auction procured only 774 MW of new generation and uprates, 
consisting of 350.7 MW UCAP from new generation and 423.6 MW UCAP from uprates.19  
The 2028/29 auction procured even less—only 524.7 MW UCAP, consisting of 317.1 MW 
UCAP from new generation and 207.6 MW UCAP from uprates.20  In both instances, the 
auctions failed to procure sufficient capacity to meet the required reserve margin.  
Customers are paying drastically more for (largely) existing generation capacity.  
This shortfall persisted even though prices reached maximum levels21 in both 
auctions, meaning that customers are paying record prices—and incumbent generation 
 
19 PJM Auction Procures 134,479 MW of Generation Resources, PJM INSIDE LINES (Dec. 17, 
2025), 
https://insidelines.pjm.com/pjm-auction-procures-134479-mw-of-generation-resources/ 
(“Dec. 17, 2025 PJM Auction Procures 134,479 MW of Generation Res. as Work Continues To 
Address Growing Elec. Demand”). 
20 PJM Capacity Auction Procures 138,318 MW of Generation Res. as Work Continues To Address 
Growing Elec. Demand, PJM INSIDE LINES (July 14, 2026), https://insidelines.pjm.com/pjm-
capacity-auction-procures-138318-mw-of-generation-resources-as-work-continues-to-address-
growing-electricity-demand (“July 14, 2026 PJM Capacity Auction Procures 138,318 MW of 
Generation Res. as Work Continues To Address Growing Elec. Demand”). 
21 In both the 2027/28 Base Residual Auction and the 2028/29 Base Residual Auction, prices 
reached and were constrained by the price cap set by the Commission.  See Dec. 17, 2025 PJM 
Auction Procures 134,479 MW of Generation Res. as Work Continues To Address Growing Elec. 
Demand (“The price came in at the FERC-approved cap, $333.44/MW-day (UCAP) for the entire 
PJM footprint . . . .”); July 14, 2026 PJM Capacity Auction Procures 138,318 MW of Generation 
Res. as Work Continues To Address Growing Elec. Demand (“The price came in at the FERC-
approved cap, $325/MW-day (UCAP) for the entire PJM footprint,” and noting “the third 
consecutive auction with the price collar”).

8 
owners are reaping benefits—while reliability risks mount.  EEI members in the region feel 
a specific urgency to resolve these critical issues because they have an obligation to serve 
customers in the region, unlike almost all other members and stakeholders in the region. 
These market failures reinforce EEI’s central point:  even a faster and more 
transparent stakeholder process cannot procure capacity that the market’s price signals are 
not calling forth, which is why governance reform must proceed alongside, and in service 
of, substantive market reform.  Such reforms should include a commitment to developing 
a more flexible and nimble approach to procurement.22  
As the Commission evaluates changes to governance and stakeholder processes, 
EEI urges that it remain focused on the larger goal of accelerating the development of 
supply and transmission infrastructure to ensure reliable service to customers in the region. 
III. 
EEI MEMBERS STAND READY TO PLAY A PRODUCTIVE ROLE 
EEI and its members in the PJM region have worked, and will continue to work, 
productively with PJM, state policymakers, the Commission, and others to ensure that the 
region’s 67 million consumers continue to enjoy reliable and affordable service.  Efforts to 
reform governance and stakeholder processes are a welcome step in the right direction 
toward solving the larger resource adequacy challenges PJM and customers in the region 
face.  EEI urges the Commission to act with speed and to pursue governance reform as a

customers-and-ensure-data-centers-pay-fair-share; see also Letter from Drew Maloney, President 
& CEO of EEI (Oct. 7, 2025), https://www.eei.org//-/media/Project/EEI/Documents/Resources-
and-Media/Newsroom/FINAL-Letter---EEI-to-OPSI-PJM_100725_PJM-Execs.pdf.

9 
necessary complement to—not a substitute for—the fundamental market and state-policy 
changes required to resolve the region’s resource adequacy crisis. 
 
Respectfully submitted, 
 
   /s/
